title: Delta Signal Ownership and Triage Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for owning performance delta signals end-to-end: from alert to root cause candidate, including what to capture, how to split cohorts for canary comparisons, and a pragmatic bisect protocol for shipping fixes quickly.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: on-call SREs, runtime engineers, and applied ML owners.
- Scope: transient and persistent latency/throughput regressions impacting hosted and dedicated deployments. Excludes large-scale infra outages (network/region down) unless correlated.

Principles (short):
- Capture the smallest reproducible delta: time window, traffic cohort, model/version, hardware class.
- Prefer signal triangulation (traces + metrics + payload sampling) over single-metric conclusions.
- Fast hypothesis -> lightweight experiment loop (canary, revert, config tweak).

Signal taxonomy (fields we always record):
- service.route, model.name, model.version, hw.class (A100-V2, T4), seq.len.p50/p95, batch.size, kv-cache-hit-rate, request.path (API vs internal), ingestion-region, client-tier (free/prod).

Initial triage checklist (first 20 minutes):
1) Confirm alert validity: check dashboard window vs baseline, verify no dashboard data dropouts.
2) Snapshot top-5 slow routes (p95) and top-10 callers by QPS.
3) Grab two traces: a slow trace and a baseline fast trace for same route; attach trace IDs to incident.
4) Check recent deploys (service, model, infra) in last 6 hours. Capture PR numbers.
5) Inspect resource saturation: GPU util, CPU, memory, network, NVMe.
6) Check KV cache evictions and prefix cache hit-rate.
7) If candidate commit exists, mark as hypothesis and start controlled canary.

Dashboard queries and examples (templates to paste):
- p95 latency by model: SELECT time_bucket('1m', ts) AS t, model_version, percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) FROM requests WHERE ts > now() - interval '2h' GROUP BY t, model_version ORDER BY t DESC;
- KV cache hit-rate: sum(kv_hits) / nullif(sum(kv_lookups),0) by minute;
- Batch size distribution (histogram) for route: histogram(batch_size) FROM request_metrics where route = 'generate' and ts > now()-interval '1h'

Bisect protocol (fast, low-friction):
- Objective: determine whether the regression maps to a set of commits, a model change, a config flip, or traffic mix.
- If suspect commit range exists (timebox), run a binary-search deploy on a canary pool (10% capacity):
  1) Deploy midpoint commit to canary pool with traffic mirror (no rollout) and synthetic workload with representative prompts.
  2) If canary reproduces p95 delta > threshold, bisect lower half; otherwise test upper half.
  3) Each bisect iteration must capture: perf snapshot, trace sample, kernel-level logs, and KV cache metrics.
  4) Stop when you narrow to <= 3 commits or 1 config change.
- If no git suspect: pivot to traffic/cohort bisect (see cohort section).

Canary cohort comparison method (structured):
- Cohort axes: model.version, sequence-length-bucket (short/med/long), hw.class, customer-tier, payload-type (system vs user tokens).
- For a paired comparison, reserve two identical sparse pools (A and B). Route 5% traffic to B with suspected change, 5% to A baseline. Capture these artifacts for 30m: token-level latencies, trace samples, GPU profiles.
- Analysis: compute delta per-cohort (p50/p95/p99), delta in token-per-second, and delta in KV cache hit-rate. If deltas concentrate in one cohort (e.g., long sequences on T4) that guides root cause hunting.

Profiling artifacts (what to capture):
- lightweight: flamegraph from 1-2 slow requests (user and system stacks), top-threads CPU, GPU occupancy sample (nvidia-smi pmon).
- deep: kernel traces (cupti/Nsight), memory allocator stats, allocator fragmentation snapshots, and compiled-kernel selection log.

Hypothesis journal (how to log):
- hypothesis:id-<short> | short sentence | confidence (low/med/high) | tests run (links) | outcome | next action.
Example: hypothesis:id-73 | attention-kernel-change-introduced-regression | med | canary-2026-02-18-10:30 (trace ids...), perf-snapshot-2026-02-18 | failed to reproduce in canary -> deprioritize.

Escalation and ownership matrix:
- Triage owner (default SRE on call) -> owns initial checklist.
- Runtime engineer -> owns bisect and kernel-level artifacts.
- Model-owner -> owns model experiments and quantization regressions.
- Pager escalation: 30 min if no progress -> call runtime lead; 90 min if customer-impacting -> page exec on-call.

Dev-time experiments (fast mitigation knobs):
- Force fallback to compatible kernel (if available).
- Reduce max-batch or disable adaptive-batching for suspect route.
- Temporarily pin older model variant.
- Increase cache TTL for cold-start heavy clients.

Postmortem signals to capture (for future):
- precise commit(s) and PRs, canary vs baseline artifact bundles, flamegraphs, perf snapshots, KV cache deltas, operator actions and timestamps.

Open questions and follow-ups (TODOs):
- Add standard synthetic prompt set for sequence-length edge cases.
- Automate paired canary cohorts creation in console with single button.
- Build a small CLI to perform bisect loop and automatically upload artifacts to the incident folder.

Next actions (near term):
- (Aisha) wire up a saved dashboard with the queries above and add to incident rotation.
- (Jordan) prototype the paired-cohort canary automation by EOW.
- (Marcus) document the perf snapshot format so artifacts are comparable across incidents.

Notes to self (rough):
- keep artifact names consistent: incident-<date>-<route>-<cohort>.zip
- when in doubt always attach one slow & one fast trace to the incident ticket.

End of working draft.
